name: Latvian
variety: Standard Latvian (based on the Central dialect). The codified norm has three syllable tones, as in the Vidzeme varieties around Valmiera and Cēsis; most speakers, including those in Rīga, distinguish two.
sources: Laua, Alise (1997). Latviešu literārās valodas fonētika. Rīga: Zvaigzne ABC.
Nau, Nicole (1998). Latvian. München: Lincom Europa.
Nītiņa, Daina & Grigorjevs, Juris (eds.) (2013). Latviešu valodas gramatika. Rīga: LU Latviešu valodas institūts.
Grigorjevs, Juris (2008). Latviešu valodas patskaņu sistēmas akustisks un auditīvs raksturojums. Rīga: LU Latviešu valodas institūts.
Grigorjevs, Juris & Jaroslavienė, Jurgita (2015). Comparative study of the qualitative features of the Lithuanian and Latvian monophthongs. Baltistica 50(1).
Kariņš, A. Krišjānis (1996). The Prosodic Structure of Latvian. PhD dissertation, University of Pennsylvania.
Dogil, Grzegorz (1999). Baltic languages. In H. van der Hulst (ed.), Word Prosodic Systems in the Languages of Europe. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Ekblom, Richard (1933). Die lettischen Akzentarten. Uppsala: Almqvist & Wiksell.
Balode, Laimute & Holvoet, Axel (2001). The Latvian language and its dialects. In Ö. Dahl & M. Koptjevskaja-Tamm (eds.), The Circum-Baltic Languages, vol. 1. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Holst, Jan Henrik (2001). Lettische Grammatik. Hamburg: Buske.
contrasts: phonemic vowel length in stressed and unstressed syllables (kazas 'goats' vs kāzas 'wedding'; final -a vs -ā)
narrow /e eː/ versus wide /æ æː/, both written e, ē
three syllable tones on long syllables in the codified norm: level, falling, broken (loks 'leek' level, loks 'arc' falling, logs 'window' broken; zāle 'hall' level vs zāle 'grass' broken)
palatal /c ɟ ɲ ʎ/ (ķ, ģ, ņ, ļ) versus /k ɡ n l/
voiced versus voiceless obstruents, kept word-finally
the letter o stands for the diphthong /uo/ in native words and for /ɔ/ or /ɔː/ in loanwords
allophony: a voiceless obstruent between a short stressed vowel and a following vowel is lengthened (lapa [ˈlapːa], aka [ˈakːa], upe [ˈupːe]); this lengthening is automatic, not contrastive
obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member, also word-finally before the ending -s (labs [laps], gads [ɡats], mazs [mass], logs [luoks], atbilde [ˈadbilde])
no devoicing of a single word-final voiced obstruent (daudz [daud͡z])
/v/ is the glide [u̯] after a vowel at the end of a syllable (tev [teu̯], zivs [ziu̯s], tēvs [tæːu̯s]); /j/ is [i̯] in the same position
sonorants after a short vowel in the same syllable are lengthened and carry part of the syllable tone (balts, kalns)
the choice of narrow or wide e depends mainly on the following syllable: wide before back vowels, narrow before front vowels and palatals, with many morphological exceptions
short vowels in final unstressed syllables are weakened or devoiced in colloquial speech
/t d n l s z/ are dental or alveolar; /r/ is an alveolar trill; /x f/ and /ɔ ɔː/ occur only in loanwords
phonotactics: syllable tones occur only on long syllables: long vowel, diphthong, or short vowel plus sonorant in the same syllable
geminate sonorants in a few words (mamma, ķemme); other long consonants are automatic
final clusters with -s are common (draugs, zirgs, galds)

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable; exceptions are a small set of words, mostly compounds and greetings, that are stressed on the second element (paldies, labdien, labrīt, nekad, neviens, and some words with jeb-, ik-, pus- and superlative vis-).
stress.cues: intensity and pitch; long vowels and tones occur in stressed and unstressed syllables, so duration is not a reliable cue

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in the standard; colloquial speech weakens short final vowels
rhythm.notes: Rhythm is shaped by the quantity system (short and long vowels, automatic consonant lengthening) and initial stress; the class label is an impression from the descriptive literature.

length.notes: Long vowels are about twice as long as short ones or more. Consonant length is not contrastive apart from a few geminate sonorants, but the lengthening of voiceless obstruents after a short stressed vowel is obligatory and must be produced.

intonation.declarative: highest pitch on the stressed first syllable of the prominent word, gradual fall to a low ending
intonation.yes_no_question: with the particle vai the contour can fall as in a statement; without it the pitch rises on the last stressed syllable or at the end
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: rise or high level at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: high or falling pitch beginning on the stressed initial syllable; its shape within a long syllable depends on the syllable tone
intonation.notes: Sentence intonation is described only in general terms here (low confidence).

tone.tone_bearing_unit: syllable (long syllables only; clearest in the stressed syllable)

inventory.name: level tone (stieptā intonācija), marked ˜
inventory.description: high and even or slightly rising pitch held through the whole long syllable, with even intensity
inventory.duration: long; the longest of the three

inventory.name: falling tone (krītošā intonācija), marked `
inventory.description: a short rise at the start, then pitch and intensity fall through the syllable

inventory.name: broken tone (lauztā intonācija), marked ^
inventory.description: pitch rises in the first part of the syllable, is interrupted by a glottal closure or creak, and the short second part is lower and weaker
inventory.phonation: glottal stop or creaky voice in the middle of the syllable
inventory.duration: long, with a short second part

tone.neutral_tone: short syllables carry no tone; in unstressed long syllables the tones are weaker and partly neutralised
tone.notes: Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the descriptions (Laua 1997; Ekblom 1933; Dogil 1999), not measured values. Two-tone systems are the most common: in the west, including Rīga, falling and broken have merged and contrast with level; in the east (High Latvian) level and falling have merged and contrast with broken. Tones are not written in ordinary spelling.

phonation: glottalisation (glottal stop or creak) inside syllables with the broken tone

problems: No syllable tones: level, falling and broken tone are not distinguished, there are no tone phonemes, and the glottalisation of the broken tone is missing (loks and logs differ only in k and g).

No regressive voicing assimilation: labs, gads, mazs, logs, draugs, zirgs, augt, atbilde keep the written voicing ([bs], [ds], [zs], [ɡs], [ɡt], [tb]); the translator does not set the regressive voicing option.
Voiceless obstruents after a short stressed vowel are not lengthened (lapa, aka, upe).
v is never the glide [u̯] at the end of a syllable (tēvs is [tæːʋs]).
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
good: initial stress with listed exceptions (paldies, labdien, ne- and vis- words)
phonemic vowel length from the spelling, with a nominal long to short length of about 2.4 to 1 in the phoneme table
narrow and wide e, ē ([e] vs [æ]) chosen by a large rule set (tēvs [tæːʋs], ēst [eːst])
the letter o resolved to [uo], [o] or [oː] by rules and word lists (loks, roka, valoda)
palatals ķ, ģ, ļ, ņ as single phonemes; affricates dz, dž
lengthening of sonorants after short vowels and geminate sonorants (mamma)

notes: No formant, VOT or rhythm-metric values are given because I cannot quote published figures with confidence; Grigorjevs (2008) reports formant measurements for the Latvian vowels.
